title: Raids in a Month: WoW Forever Is Racing Its Own Players to Burnout
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: 40 hours in, level 18 and a half, and 2 gold to my name. The first raids open December 9th, about a month after launch, and for a game sold on a slower pace, that schedule is pushing working players straight toward burnout.
content:
Forty hours. That's how long I've put into my Dwarf Priest. In that time I've reached level 18 and a half, and I have 2 gold and 65 silver.

Meanwhile, the first raids open on December 9th, about a month after launch. For a game that was sold on a slower, more relaxed pace, that date tells players their time doesn't matter much.

I'm not asking Blizzard to slow down the people who no-lifed to 60 in a week. I'm asking for a release schedule that doesn't punish everyone else for having jobs, kids, and a life.

The Promise Was a Slower Game

WoW Forever was pitched to people like me. We played the original or TBC years ago, and we aren't college students anymore. The talk of a relaxed pace and horizontal progression was the hook. It said you could take your time and still end up in the same place as everyone else.

I believed that. If progression really is horizontal, showing up late shouldn't matter. But the schedule says otherwise. Starting the raid clock a month in tells you the real game starts at 60, and everyone is now racing to get there.

That's not a relaxed pace. That's a deadline.

"Just Raid Later" Isn't the Answer People Think It Is

The most common reply to this complaint is simple: nobody's forcing you to raid week one. It's technically true, and it misses how the game actually works. Showing up late costs you in at least four ways.

  • The Gear Gap Compounds: Every week early raiders clear, they pull further ahead. That gap doesn't stay in the raid. It shows up in PvP, where I'm planning to spend my time, and in PUG invites, where late 60s get passed over.
  • Your Guild Won't Wait Forever: If you're not 60 when your guild starts, it has two options: replace you, or fill your spot with outsiders. Neither feels good, and both happen to the players with the least free time.
  • You Lose the Blind First Clear: Part of the magic is learning boss mechanics alongside a community that's also figuring them out. A month later, everything is solved, and you're expected to know it all before you step in.
  • The Economy Moves On Without You: Prices go up, farming spots get contested, and the players who've been sitting at 60 have had weeks to stack gold. With 2g 65s at level 18, I'm not catching up in that market.

The raids will still be there. The moment won't.

The Other Side Has a Point

To be fair, the people pushing back aren't wrong about everything.

Players who hit 60 in the first week need something to do, or they'll call the endgame dead and drift off to other games. Some of them already have exalted reps, pre-raid best-in-slot gear, and full bags of gold. Delaying raids a month wouldn't close that gap. They'd just spend the extra month farming and pull further ahead anyway.

And it's true that most of us were never competing with the top guilds. Original Classic in 2019 had Molten Core open from day one, and plenty of casual players still had a great time.

But "you'll always be behind the sweats" isn't the same as "timing doesn't matter." I'm not comparing myself to world-first guilds. I'm comparing myself to my own guildmates, the PUGs I'll be applying to, and the players I'll meet in battlegrounds. That's the gap the release date controls.

The Real Cost Is Burnout

I'll be honest: I don't enjoy leveling. I'm already theorycrafting my level 60 Priest because the endgame is what I came for. Every hour between here and there feels like a toll, and the raid date makes it feel like a toll with a late fee.

I'm not the only one. One dads-and-moms guild on Reddit described the pressure as "through the roof." Only the members who could take days off work had hit 60, and the guild worried people would burn out before they ever set foot in a raid. I already know people who've quit over this.

This matters beyond hurt feelings. A game called Forever needs players who stick around, level alts, and come back for the next phase. A schedule that burns people out on their first character kills the appetite for a second one.

What Blizzard Could Do Instead

None of this needs a total redesign. A few changes would go a long way:

  1. Push the Raids Back a Few Weeks: Even a short delay would let working players reach 60. It could also turn the opening into an event, like the army of 60s waiting at the Dark Portal for TBC.
  2. Give Early 60s Something That Isn't a Head Start: Reputations, dungeons like UBRS, world events, and PvP can keep the fast players busy without widening the gear gap.
  3. Build In Real Catch-Up: If progression is meant to be horizontal, late arrivals need a path to relevant gear that doesn't mean grinding the same content for months.
  4. Speed Up Leveling for People Who've Done It Before: Rested XP boosts or faster alt leveling would respect the time of returning players who already know the zones by heart.

Respect the Time We Have

I want to love this game. I'm 40 hours in and still logging on. But respecting players' time means designing for people who play a few hours a night, not just for the ones who can take a week off.

Right now, WoW Forever feels like it's in a hurry. The players it was built for aren't.

title: Priest Crafted Tier Set Stats Revealed: Raiments and Vestments of Conviction
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: A hotfix revealed the stats for the crafted versions of the first raid tier in Forever. Here's what Shadow and Healing Priests are getting from the Raiments and Vestments of Conviction, and why the set bonuses still need work.
content:
The first raid tier in World of Warcraft: Forever doesn't open until December 9th, but we already have our first real look at Priest tier gear. A hotfix revealed the stats for the crafted tier pieces, and Priests have two sets: the Raiments of Conviction for Shadow and the Vestments of Conviction for Healing.

Blizzard has confirmed this wasn't a leak. Item obfuscation only hides gear that drops from raid bosses. Items that come from vendors and recipes aren't covered, so these stats are showing up in game on purpose. Blizzard also confirmed the set bonuses are placeholders and will change before release.

Each set has six pieces in total, but only four of them have been revealed so far: legs, shoulders, hands, and feet. That's eight pieces across both sets.

One Crafted Piece, and That's It

Every one of these pieces has the same tag: Unique-Equipped: Artisan's Tier (1). That means you can only wear one crafted tier piece at a time.

Tier is going to drop across all three raids, but not everyone has a 40-man guild, and even the ones who do get unlucky. One crafted piece looks like Blizzard's version of bad luck protection. If you're one piece short of your next set bonus, you craft the missing slot and you're there.

Raiments of Conviction (Shadow)

ItemSlotArmorStaminaIntellectSpiritNature ResBonus Stats
Pants of ConvictionLegs8120181091% spell crit, +15 spell damage and healing
Mantle of ConvictionShoulder701417-70.9% spell hit, +13 spell damage and healing
Gloves of ConvictionHands581511-7+11 spell damage and healing, 5 spell penetration
Treads of ConvictionFeet6414121170.9% spell hit, +13 spell damage and healing

Set bonuses (placeholder):

  • (2) Set: 1% spell hit.
  • (3) Set: Shackle Undead lasts 10 seconds longer.
  • (4) Set: Up to 21 spell damage when fighting Undead.
  • (5) Set: Devouring Plague cooldown reduced by 60 seconds.

Vestments of Conviction (Healing)

ItemSlotArmorStaminaIntellectSpiritNature ResBonus Stats
Leggings of ConvictionLegs811916209+33 healing, +11 damage
Pauldrons of ConvictionShoulder701511137+32 healing, +11 damage
Handguards of ConvictionHands581412117+20 healing, +6 damage, 5 mana per 5 sec
Boots of ConvictionFeet641421-7+24 healing, +8 damage

Set bonuses (placeholder):

  • (2) Set: +10 Spirit.
  • (3) Set: Fear Ward cooldown reduced by 60 seconds.
  • (4) Set: Up to 26 healing and 9 damage.
  • (5) Set: Penance and Prayer of Mending cooldowns reduced by 1 second.

My Take

The stats look solid. The healing set is loaded with Spirit and healing power, and the Shadow set finally gives us real hit and spell damage on every piece. After weeks of complaining about the lack of Spell Power gear while leveling, it's good to see Shadow getting gear built for Shadow.

The set bonuses are a different story, and it's obvious why Blizzard is calling them placeholders. Shadow's 5-piece cuts 60 seconds off Devouring Plague, but Devouring Plague's cooldown is already down to 24 seconds. You can't cut 60 seconds off a 24-second cooldown. Two of the Shadow bonuses are also built around Undead, which is great if the raid is full of Undead and useless if it isn't. Healing's bonuses make a lot more sense, but a 1-second cooldown cut on Penance and Prayer of Mending isn't much for a 5-piece.

Also notice that every single piece has Nature Resistance on it. Blizzard hasn't said anything about the bosses, but they didn't put that stat on both sets for no reason. I'd expect some Nature damage in that first tier.

Where Do You Get the Recipes?

Right now, nobody knows. On the beta, the recipes were bought from Aisarra Nightmeadow with Malleable Essence of Nature. In the latest Forever build, she doesn't sell them anymore. Blizzard hasn't said whether they'll come back to her, or if there will be new ways to earn them once the raids open.

As for the tier pieces that drop from bosses, don't expect to see those stats early. They'll most likely stay hidden until the raid opens on December 9th and people start pulling them off bosses.

title: Krol'dok Stronghold Key Guide: Unlock the Shortcut to Overlord Mugg
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Krol'dok Stronghold has a key quest that lets you skip straight to the final boss on future runs. Here's where the quest drops, what mats to bring, and where the shortcut is.
content:
Forever added nine new dungeons, and Krol'dok Stronghold is hiding one of the best quality of life rewards out of all of them. Inside the dungeon is a quest chain that ends with a key, and that key opens doors that cut a big chunk out of every future run.

If you're planning on running this place more than once, you want this key.

How to Start the Quest

The quest starts from an item, not a quest giver. Kill Tunk inside the dungeon and he'll drop the item that starts Krol'dok Moulding.

Take it out of the dungeon to Riverglades and turn it in:

  • Horde: Kreza Darkthorn in Rog'mar.
  • Alliance: Alphonse Dumas in Farholde Keep.

Bring Your Mats Ahead of Time

Turning in Krol'dok Moulding unlocks the follow-up, Key Ingredients. It asks for:

  • Thick Leather: 4
  • Iron Bar: 12

Here's the tip: get these before you ever step into the dungeon. If you already have them in your bags when you turn in the first quest, you can complete Key Ingredients on the spot and walk away with the Krol'dok Compound Key right then. No second trip, no waiting on the Auction House.

Both quests together give around 7,000 XP, which is a nice bonus on top of the key.

Using the Key

Once you have the Krol'dok Compound Key, head back into Krol'dok Stronghold. The key opens two doors that create a shortcut to the final boss, Overlord Mugg.

The first door is right behind the second boss, Twilight Commander Zarmok. Kill him, use the key, and keep moving.

Worth Remembering

I know a ton of people are still under level 40 right now, so this might not matter to you yet. But keep it in mind. When you get there, grab the mats early, kill Tunk, and get the key on your first run. Every run after that gets shorter, and with how slow leveling is in Forever, anything that saves time is worth it.

title: Blizzard Admits Spell Power Gear Is Too Thin While Leveling, and More Is on the Way
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Kris Zierhut admitted Forever didn't ship with enough Spell Power gear for leveling casters, especially from 15 to 40. More is coming in future patches, and as a Priest, I can't wait.
content:
Every caster leveling in Forever has felt it. You finish a quest, check the reward, and it's another piece of gear with nothing a caster cares about. Now the developers have finally owned up to it.

On the newest WoW: Forever Podcast, Kris Zierhut and Aidan Moon talked about the Spell Power problem, and Kris came right out and said it: there isn't enough of it in the game right now.

Why This Is a Bigger Deal in Forever

Casters in Forever took a hit to their baseline damage. That wasn't an accident. The plan was for gear to make up the difference, so Mages, Warlocks, Priests, and every other caster would care about their gear the same way Warriors and Rogues do.

That's a good idea on paper. But if you lower our damage and then don't give us the gear to get it back, all you've done is make leveling slower. And for a lot of casters, that's exactly what's been happening.

What Kris Said

Here's how he explained it on the podcast:

"As you're leveling up a spellcaster, you really don't care about your gear that much, and I really wanted to fix that problem and make spell casters care as much about their gear as Warriors and Rogues do.... That being said, I think there probably is not enough Spell Power gear leveling up. As I was introducing it, the design team was very wary of how much change it was, and I probably added a little bit less of it than we should. So going into future patches, I want to be adding more spell power gear for alts as you're leveling up in that 15-40 range where it's thinner than it ought to be."

So the gear does exist, and you can find it today. There just isn't nearly enough of it, and the gap is worst from level 15 to 40. That's pretty much the whole middle of the leveling experience.

As a Priest: Yes Please

I'll be honest. This is great news. We need this.

  • Leveling Gets Better: More Spell Power gear means our damage actually grows as we level, instead of feeling stuck until 40.
  • Gear Finally Feels Exciting: Getting an upgrade should feel good. Right now most quest rewards are a shrug for casters.
  • Cool Sets to Chase: I want to see Priests running around in sets that actually look good and do something for us. That's something to look forward to while leveling, not just a number going up.

It's not a fix today, and that's frustrating if you're grinding a caster through the teens and twenties right now. But Kris admitted the problem, explained why it happened, and said it's getting fixed. That's more than we usually get.

Now Blizzard has to actually follow through. Give casters the gear we were promised when they cut our damage, and leveling a Priest will feel a whole lot better.

title: Blizzard Wants to Kill BiS in WoW Forever, and I'm All For It
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: No more one-size-fits-all gear list. Zirene wants creature types and biomes to decide what your best gear is for every fight in Forever, and the cookie cutter BiS spreadsheet is finally on the chopping block.
content:
Zirene just said what a lot of us have been thinking for years. On the newest WoW: Forever Podcast, the developer made it clear he's done with Best in Slot, and he's building the game's gear around that idea.

You know how it works. Somebody posts the list, everyone of your class follows it, and a month later every Priest in the raid is wearing the same robe, the same trinkets, and the same wand. People have been min-maxing that way since vanilla, hitting their stat caps and stacking whatever number goes highest. Forever is trying to break that habit.

What Zirene Said

Here's how he put it on the podcast:

"I essentially want to get rid of 'BiS'. I think that 'BiS' is not a good thing for a video game that's supposed to be about role-playing systems about it. That's why I've introduced the creature subtype system, the biome system, and in the raid, it's different... In the raid, if you go to the left wing, that's 'snowy'; if you go to the right wing, that's 'haunted', so different parts of the raid will have different biomes. So I think your BiS should be different for every single boss if you're actually making a theoretical BiS list. It should be based on the creature and the biome. Itemization is 'I don't want you to think about BiS'; I just want you to think about the fight in front of you and how you're going to fight it."

So instead of one gear set that's best everywhere, the best gear changes depending on what you're fighting and where you're fighting it. A snowy wing and a haunted wing in the same raid can call for completely different items.

Zirene was clear that this isn't only for the min-maxers. It works for the players who love building a perfect list for every single boss, and it works for the player who picked up some weird niche item while leveling and finally gets a fight where it shines.

Of course, carrying a different set of gear for every creature type and biome means your bags are going to explode. The devs knew that one was coming and said bigger bags and better item search and sorting are on the way, since they plan to keep adding more of these items. Until then, go grab that free Red Bag.

Why I'm All For It

I completely agree with this. BiS means everyone chases the same cookie cutter build. Same items, same stats, zero creativity. You look up the list, you farm the list, and you end up looking exactly like every other player of your class.

  • Creativity Actually Matters: When the best gear depends on the fight, you have to think about what you're walking into instead of copying a list.
  • Niche Items Get a Purpose: That odd drop sitting in your bank might actually be the right call for a specific boss.
  • Less Endless Grinding: If one item isn't the end-all for a slot, there's less pressure to farm the same boss fifty times for a tiny upgrade.

Play Your Spec, Not the Spreadsheet

Here's the part people need to hear. If your gear is close to the best, and you play your spec properly, you're going to be fine. That's healthier long term than constantly hunting for the perfect item and burning out chasing one percent upgrades.

Gear should support how you play. It shouldn't replace knowing your class. A player who knows their rotation, manages their resources, and understands the fight in front of them will outperform someone in a full BiS list who doesn't.

Blizzard is pushing players to think about the fight instead of the list. That's exactly what an RPG should be.

title: What Happened to Respecting Players' Time? Why WoW Forever Is Losing Players Before Endgame
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: 33 hours for level 17, a starved economy, overtuned dungeons, and class identity locked behind the grind. WoW Forever is losing players in the leveling experience long before they ever see endgame.
content:
World of Warcraft: Forever launched with massive promise: a fresh, evergreen classic experience built to capture the magic of progression while smoothing out the rough edges of vanilla Azeroth. Yet barely weeks into launch, a troubling trend is emerging across class Discords, community forums, and guild rosters. Players aren't quitting because of bad raids or broken endgame tuning. They are quitting because the leveling experience completely fails to respect their time.

For years, Blizzard has talked about respecting players' time, building systems where effort translates into meaningful, steady progress rather than busywork. In Forever, that philosophy seems to have vanished entirely. Right now, a player can sink 33 hours into a single character and barely reach level 17. That isn't an immersive classic journey. It's an unsustainable slog.

Across virtually every class community, the drop-off is already visible. Players roll in excited to theorycraft, run group content, and build toward endgame, only to hit a wall of tedium, overtuned friction, and economic frustration right out of the starting zones that drains their momentum before their toolkit even comes online.

33 Hours for Level 17: A Slog From the Start

The pacing problem in Forever isn't isolated to one late-game bracket. It drags across the entire 1-60 journey. From the very first zones onward, the experience curve feels artificially stretched out just to pad playtime metrics.

Instead of steady, rewarding momentum, every single level turns into an uphill trudge:

  • Punishing Quest Drop Rates: Killing 40 mobs to collect 8 quest items while competing against three other players tagging the exact same spawns isn't challenging gameplay. It's a slot machine that wastes hours of your life in starter and mid-level zones alike.
  • Endless Travel Time: Between running everywhere on foot for the first 40 levels and constantly bouncing across zones just to piece together enough quests for a single bar of XP, a massive chunk of that 33-hour playtime is spent simply walking from point A to point B rather than actually playing the game.

The Irony of Mass Bans vs. Economic Design

Developers are cracking down hard on gold buying with mass bans, acting like they are protecting the game's integrity. But punishing players for buying gold completely ignores the root cause: the game's design is actively manufacturing the demand for it.

When you create a starved economy where basic survival costs are absurdly inflated, you push players toward desperation:

  • Overpriced Everything: Skill training, crafting materials, and mount costs are priced like luxury goods relative to the copper and silver earned while leveling.
  • The Repair Trap: Between overtuned leveling dungeons that cause constant wipes and skyrocketing repair bills, playing group content actively puts characters into debt.

When players hit a wall where progression feels mathematically out of reach without an army of farming hours, people look for shortcuts. If developers want to stop gold buying, putting strict caps on Auction House items and rebalancing baseline costs would solve the problem overnight. Treating the symptom while ignoring an oppressive economic framework only frustrates the player base further.

The Dungeon XP Buff That Backfired

On paper, increasing dungeon experience by 50% sounds like a step in the right direction, until you factor in the catch. Alongside the XP bump, dungeons were tuned to be significantly harder, turning routine leveling runs into grueling, wipe-heavy marathons.

When you combine overtuned dungeon trash and bosses with a starved economy, the math breaks down fast:

  • Slower Clear Times Cancel Out the Buff: A 50% XP increase means very little when pulls take twice as long, require constant drinking and crowd control, or fall apart mid-run after a couple of wipes.
  • Repair Bills You Can't Afford: When players are already scraping by for copper just to train their spells, wiping in overtuned leveling dungeons actively sets them backward financially. Group content ends up feeling like a risk rather than an efficient alternative to questing.

Class Identity Delayed Across the Board

Players stick with an MMO when their character feels fun to press buttons on. In Forever, spending 30+ hours just to hit level 17 means spending weeks playing an incomplete, watered-down version of your class. Whether you're a Warrior starved for rage and weapons, a caster locked into repetitive wand and single-button rotations, or a hybrid forced to pick between soloing and group utility until Dual Spec is finally affordable, you're stuck waiting on your actual class to show up.

When core rotational abilities, resource sustain talents, and build-defining mechanics are buried deep in the talent trees, the entire 1-60 climb feels less like an adventure and more like a massive unpaid tax every class has to grind through just to unlock their actual character.

The "Journey" Defense vs. Reality

Defenders of Forever's pacing argue that the slow grind, harsh gold scarcity, and punishing tuning are intentional. Their argument is that modern WoW trained players to rush to max level, and Forever is meant to be savored over months rather than days. There is truth to that philosophy. A slower world can create stronger social bonds and make hitting level 60 feel meaningful.

However, tedium is not difficulty, and artificial poverty is not depth. Taking 33 hours to hit level 17 while struggling to afford basic spells, repair bills, and a mount doesn't test a player's skill. It tests their tolerance for frustration. When dedicated players across every class are logging off in their teens and twenties and leaving community Discords entirely, the "journey" isn't building a healthier endgame. It's starving it of players before it even starts. Video games are supposed to be an escape from real life, not a second, more dreadful job.

What Needs to Change

Forever doesn't need to turn into a six-hour retail speedrun to respect its players' time. A few targeted adjustments could save the leveling curve without sacrificing the spirit of the world:

  1. Recalibrate the 1-60 XP Curve: Bring pacing back to a place where 30+ hours of play reflects real, tangible progression, not barely clearing the starter zones.
  2. Fix the Economy and Cap AH Inflation: Rebalance early gold generation, lower absurd costs for mount training and skill books, and implement reasonable caps on Auction House items to stop out-of-control inflation.
  3. Align Dungeon Difficulty With Leveling Pacing: Keep the 50% dungeon XP boost, but dial back the over-tuning on leveling dungeons so runs feel rewarding and approachable rather than a gold-draining wipe fest.
  4. Fix Quest Flow and Drop Rates: Tighten hub-to-hub progression and buff low quest item drop rates so players spend their time fighting and progressing rather than running back and forth or farming empty spawns.

Until the climb from 1 to 60 actually respects the hours and effort players put into it, Forever risks losing the exact community members who keep class hubs, guilds, and endgame rosters alive.

title: The Auction House Deposit Is Finally Back to 1 Copper, and It Never Should Have Been 1 Silver
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: With this week's reset, Blizzard finally dropped the Auction House minimum deposit from 1 Silver back to 1 Copper. It's the right call, but it took almost two weeks of players eating deposits worth more than their items to get here.
content:
It took almost two weeks, but Blizzard finally fixed it. With this week's reset, the Auction House minimum deposit in World of Warcraft: Forever is back down to 1 Copper. No more paying 1 Silver just to list an item, no matter how cheap it is.

I'm glad it's done. But it never should have shipped like this in the first place.

A Ridiculous Tax on Low-Level Players

Since launch, every single auction cost at least 1 Silver to post. That might not sound like much at level 60, but early in the game it was a joke. Most of the materials you gather in the starting zones sell for a few copper each. Paying 1 Silver to list them meant the deposit was often worth more than the item itself.

So what did people do? They stopped listing. Cloth, herbs, ore, and leather went straight to the vendor, because posting them on the Auction House was a guaranteed loss. The players who needed silver the most, fresh characters with empty bags and no gold, were the ones getting hit the hardest.

Blizzard said over a week ago that the deposit would be lowered. Then we all had to sit through another week of it before the change actually went live with the reset.

How Deposits Work Now

On the faction Auction Houses, the deposit is back to being based on the item's vendor price and how long you list it:

  • 2 Hours: 5% of vendor price.
  • 8 Hours: 20% of vendor price.
  • 24 Hours: 60% of vendor price.

That's how it should be. Cheap items cost almost nothing to list, and expensive items cost more. Your deposit actually matches what you're selling.

Why This Matters

  • Low-Level Materials Are Worth Listing Again: Stuff that sells for a few copper isn't a guaranteed loss anymore.
  • Less Risk on Unsold Auctions: If something doesn't sell, you lose a few copper instead of a full Silver every time.
  • More Supply for Crafters and Levelers: When people stop vendoring their materials, everyone else has something to buy.

Get It Right the First Time

This is a good change, and Blizzard deserves credit for making it. But a flat 1 Silver deposit on every listing was an obvious problem from day one. Anyone who leveled a fresh character could have told them that. Players shouldn't have to spend two weeks losing money on every auction before a basic economy setting gets fixed.

Leveling in Forever is already slow. The last thing new players need is the Auction House punishing them for trying to make a few coins. Now it doesn't. Go list your Linen Cloth.

title: WoW Forever: Free 16-Slot Red Bag and Sun Shades Transmog From the Former Shockwave Questline
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: The Season of Discovery Warrior questline for the Shockwave rune is now open to every class in Forever. It rewards a free 16-slot Red Bag, the Sun Shades transmog, and the mysterious Ingenious Toy.
content:
Plenty of Season of Discovery questlines have made the jump to Forever, and the Warrior questline for the Shockwave rune is one of them. There's one big change, though: in Forever, the questline is open to every class, not just Warriors.

The Rewards

Halfway through the chain, you'll earn the Red Bag, a free 16-slot bag. There's one catch: equipping it lowers your effective stealth level by 2. That only matters for Rogues and Druids, so everyone else can use it with no downside.

The bag isn't the only prize. The chain ends with Rift Away, which pits you against Harvest Golem V000-A, an elite with more than 200,000 health. Defeating it rewards:

  • Sun Shades: A unique transmog item.
  • Ingenious Toy: A crafting reagent from Season of Discovery.

In Season of Discovery, the Ingenious Toy could be combined with other reagents to craft an item. What it does in Forever is still unknown.

How to Complete the Questline

  1. Find the mech. Head to the Half-Buried Mech at /way 59.2 91.5, just off the southern coast of Tanaris. Click it twice to accept and complete Beach Bot, which rewards the Guided Buoyancy Accelerant.
  2. Swim for the island. Accept Mechanical Romance and look for a lighthouse in the distance. Drink the potion and swim toward it. When you reach the edge of the map where fatigue begins, you'll spot a small island ahead. Swim straight for it.
  3. Meet Sebastian. Turn the quest in to Sebastian Jurgens on the island, then pick up Frosty Favors.
  4. Head to Everlook. Travel to Winterspring and turn in the quest to Nami at /way 61.2 37.0.
  5. Retrieve the Red Bag. Accept Red Bag Blues and go to Burning Steppes. Climb the mountain starting at /way 59.0 29.0 to reach a remote camp to the north at /way 53.0 24.8, where you'll find the Red Bag.
  6. Collect the parts. Pick up Poacher's Den and kill the level 59 Blackrock Bootleggers and Sulfuron Smugglers for the Vertically Composited Patch Hampler and the Brass-fitted Flam-Tamp Flange. Some parts can also be found on the ground.
  7. Return to Everlook. Turn the quest in to receive the book Fantastic Inventions, then accept Bookin' it Back, which sends you back to the island off Tanaris.
  8. Take the teleporter. The follow-up quest, Rift Away, opens with some roleplay. Follow Sebastian down to the teleporter, which will send you to either Westfall or Tirisfal Glades.
  9. Summon the golem. Talk to Sebastian again and press the button to summon Harvest Golem V000-A. With over 200,000 health, this elite is no pushover. Bring at least one healer and a DPS friend or two.

The Harvest Golem V000-A Fight

The encounter has three phases:

  • Phase 1: Interrupt the golem's casts.
  • Phase 2: Kite the golem until its armor stacks fall off.
  • Phase 3: Use defensive cooldowns to survive its hits and finish it off.

Once the golem is down, loot the Mech Arm on the ground to claim your rewards!

Got a questline you want covered? Send it my way and it might end up on the site.

title: Pug Paladin Rage Quits, Runs Off Alone, and Dies
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Our Paladin party leader spammed pings, got the group killed, and got outdamaged by a Priest all night. The Priest saved him anyway. Then he closed the doors, typed "l8er loosers," ran off alone, and died.
content:
Every World of Warcraft: Forever player has met him by now. He's in your group, he's running the show, and he's absolutely sure he's the main character. Tonight I got to watch one of these guys fall apart in real time, and I had a front row seat from the top of the damage meter.

A Paladin was leading our group, setting the pace and making the calls. The run lasted just under an hour, people rotated in and out along the way, and by the end seven different players had shown up on the meters. Normal pug life, until it wasn't.

The Meters Don't Lie

I was on my Priest, and I topped the damage chart on every single pull. By the end of the run, the overall numbers looked like this:

  • Priest (me): 50K damage, 38% of the group total.
  • Paladin (our fearless leader): 35K damage, 26% of the group total.
  • Everyone else: 16K damage and under.

That's a 15K gap over almost an hour, pull after pull. I'm not going to pretend that wasn't satisfying.

Priests Aren't Just Utility

There's a narrative going around Forever that Priests are a utility class. Bring one for heals, Fortitude, and maybe a dispel, and let the "real" damage dealers handle the killing. These meters say otherwise.

  • Not a Fluke: This wasn't one lucky pull or a single big crit padding the numbers. It was the overall chart for a run of almost an hour.
  • Top Every Fight: 38% of the group's damage, first on the meter every fight, and a 15K lead over the next player.
  • Sustained Damage: That kind of output only comes from playing the class well from the first pull to the last, managing your rotation and your mana the whole way.

A Priest who knows their class isn't dead weight on damage. They can lead the chart. So the next time someone tells you to roll something else if you want to do damage, send them this.

Ping, Ping, Ping

The damage meter wasn't the only thing our Paladin was leading. Turns out he was watching those meters too, and getting outdamaged by a Priest, every pull, in a group he was leading, was clearly eating at him. It showed in how he played:

  • Ping Spam: He spent the run spamming pings like the map owed him money.
  • Reckless Pulls: He dragged the group into fights it wasn't ready for.
  • Getting People Killed: By the end of the run, players were dying because of it.

And when it all went sideways at the end of the run, guess who kept him alive? The Priest he'd been salty at all night. I could have let him drop. I didn't. I saved his life.

The Meltdown

As the run wound down, he closed the doors on the rest of us, dropped a final "l8er loosers" in party chat, and took off running.

He didn't make it far. A few seconds later, the chat log delivered the punchline every one of us was waiting for: the Paladin has died.

Think about that for a second. Minutes earlier, his life was in my hands, and I kept him standing. Then he walked away from the one player keeping him alive, and the floor got him. Alone, no heals, nobody around to rez him. You genuinely can't write it better than that.

The rest of us just kept playing. One of the group picked up Treaty of Understanding and moved right along to the next quest like nothing happened. No drama, no speeches, just the game.

Priests Decide Who Lives

Leveling in Forever is slow right now, and long runs wear people down. Everyone has a bad night. But if your group is carrying the run with you, the move is to say thanks, leave the group, and log off. Closing doors on people and sprinting off with a goodbye insult just ends with you in a graveyard while the rest of the party finishes the content.

Be the player people want to group with again. And if you want proof that Priests can carry the meters, come hang out in the Discord.

Because at the end of the day, Priests are the grim reaper of every group. We decide who lives and who dies. He found out what happens when you run from yours.

Got a dungeon horror story of your own? Send it my way and it might end up on the site.

title: Blizzard Cracks Down on Blackmaw Hold Gold Exploit
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Following a weekend loot table bug in Blackmaw Hold, Blizzard has patched the dungeon, stripped illicit gold from exploiters, and issued account suspensions.
content:
Preserving the game economy is a top priority for the development team as players push into higher-level content in World of Warcraft: Forever. Over the weekend, players discovered a large pack of non-elite enemies inside the Blackmaw Hold dungeon that were mistakenly dropping full elite-level loot tables. Blizzard quickly patched the bug out early yesterday, and they have since been investigating the overall economic fallout.

If you happened to run the dungeon a couple of times naturally and benefited from the extra drops, your account is completely safe. However, a couple hundred players worldwide realized the loot drops were broken and spent hours exclusively farming those specific mobs to vendor the drops for massive gold payouts.

Blizzard placed temporary economy locks on those accounts yesterday while calculating the total exploitative gains. Today, the team is actively stripping away all gold earned from the exploit and handing out account suspensions to the most egregious abusers, sending a clear warning against farming obvious bugs.

title: New Cosmetic Hearthstone Discovered in WoW: Forever
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Players have uncovered the Scarlet Hearthstone in WoW: Forever, a new cosmetic Toy Box addition dropping from High General Abbendis in the Eastern Plaguelands.
content:
Cosmetic Hearthstones are officially live in World of Warcraft: Forever, offering unique visual animations during your 10-second cast time. The very first one has now been tracked down by players: the Scarlet Hearthstone.

Reportedly dropping from High General Abbendis in the Eastern Plaguelands, this item goes straight into your Toy Box. There is a minor catch for inventory management, though. Rather than casting directly from the Toy Box, activating the toy conjures a physical Scarlet Hearthstone item on a one-hour cooldown, meaning it will still occupy a bag slot while you carry it around. Activating it engulfs your character in scarlet flames to send you back to your home inn.

As the first cosmetic Hearthstone uncovered in Forever, it almost certainly will not be the last, leaving players on the lookout for whatever other hidden variations might be tucked away across the world.

title: November 16 Hotfixes Bring Another Priest Adjustment in WoW: Forever
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: The November 16 hotfixes reduce Vampiric Embrace party healing from 20% to 10% while doubling self-healing to keep solo survivability intact, alongside Dark Inspiration and item fixes.
content:
Priests continue to see their toolkit tweaked in the latest batch of live hotfixes deployed on November 16, 2026. While solo players will not feel a difference, Shadow Priests running in groups are seeing a notable adjustment to their passive healing output:

  • Vampiric Embrace Nerf (With Scheduled Maintenance): Healing is being reduced from 20% down to 10% of the Shadow damage dealt by the casting Priest. To compensate, the Priest receives 100% increased healing from the effect, keeping solo survivability completely intact while toning down party-wide passive healing.
  • Dark Inspiration Fix: Resolved an issue where Dark Inspiration was improperly stacking when multiple Shadow Priests were in the same party.
  • Item Fixes: Formula: Enchant Boots - Speed from reputation vendors is now properly Bind-on-Pickup, Outrider’s Gloves are functioning correctly, and The Violet Tragan will no longer break crowd control effects.

Once again, Priest group utility gets scaled back while solo play remains unchanged, continuing the ongoing trend of constant class tuning across Azeroth.

title: The new Dungeon XP Buff Is Not Enough: WoW Forever's Dungeon Design Is Alienating New and Returning Players
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Why Blizzard's 50% dungeon XP buff fails to solve deeper design flaws in WoW Forever, including overtuned difficulty, missing summoning stones, and the need for a Random Dungeon Finder.
content:
Earlier, we covered Blizzard's decision to buff dungeon mob experience by 50% after massive community backlash. While increasing experience gains is a step in the right direction to make repeating instances feel worthwhile, it completely misses a much deeper issue.

Blizzard was so hyper-focused on stopping hardcore players from spamming dungeons to rush to level 60 that they ended up creating a massive barrier to entry for everyone else. By cranking up the difficulty and stripping away basic quality-of-life features, dungeons in World of Warcraft: Forever have become needlessly punishing, even for players who outlevel the content. Simply adding more XP does not fix a system that is fundamentally broken for everyday players.

A Hostile Environment for Newcomers and Veterans Alike

A recent dungeon run perfectly illustrates the disconnect between Blizzard's design philosophy and the actual player experience. The group consisted of returning veterans who had not touched World of Warcraft in 17 years, someone who had not played since original Vanilla, and a brand-new, first-time player.

Instead of an exciting, nostalgic introduction to group content, the run was bogged down by friction from the very beginning:

  • A Confusing Group Finder: The UI is so unintuitive that the group leader did not even realize how he managed to send out the party invite. Blizzard desperately needs an actual, straightforward tutorial to walk players through basic group assembly.
  • No Summoning Stones: Without functional summoning stones outside the instances, getting everyone to the entrance is a tedious chore. Players are already quitting groups before a single pull even happens simply because the travel time and lack of convenience kill the momentum.
  • Overtuned Difficulty: Because Blizzard wanted to discourage dungeon grinding, they tuned the encounters to be overly punishing. When returning veterans and brand-new players get wiped out repeatedly even at higher levels, it stops feeling like a fun challenge and starts feeling like a brick wall.
  • Accidental Resets and Friction: After struggling just to fill the group and finally getting a fifth person into the instance, the new addition accidentally reset the entire dungeon on the party. Everyone was left frustrated and upset, turning what should have been a fun group activity into a total waste of time.

The Real Solution: A Random Dungeon Finder

If Blizzard wants to keep dungeons alive without letting people exploit them for hyper-fast leveling, the answer is not just tweaking XP numbers while leaving the dungeons miserable to assemble and clear. The solution is implementing a proper Random Dungeon Finder.

Automating the matchmaking and teleportation process removes the administrative headache of staring at a confusing tool, dealing with accidental instance resets while trying to backfill a spot, or spending twenty minutes running across continents just to watch someone drop group. Players want to log in, press a button, and play the game with others, not wrestle with outdated logistics.

Pacing vs. Player Retention

Blizzard tried to fix the perceived problem of fast leveling, and in doing so, they created a much bigger crisis. Alienating returning veterans and turning away first-time players is a guaranteed way to shrink the community.

At the end of the day, developers have to ask themselves what actually matters more: preventing a subset of players from hitting level 60 quickly, or losing massive chunks of the player base entirely. From a business standpoint, driving people away directly translates to lost subscriptions and declining profits. Beyond the bottom line, developers have a responsibility to build a welcoming, functional experience for the people investing their time into the world. Right now, punishing dungeon design is accomplishing the exact opposite.

title: WoW Forever: Priest Hotfixes Week of November 8th, 2026
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Review the latest Priest hotfixes for the week of November 8, 2026, featuring Shadowform quality of life fixes, talent interactions, and profession adjustments.
content:
Priest Class Changes

  • Shadowform: No longer breaks when casting Fear Ward.
  • Power Infusion: Will now correctly persist when used on allies.
  • Revelation: Fixed an issue where the enchant was activated by Vampiric Embrace healing.
  • Holy Nova: Fixed an issue where it was not correctly unlearned when untalenting from the spell.
  • Confounding Flash (Gnome): Can now correctly be used while in Shadowform.
  • Twilight Focus: The talent will now correctly work while in Shadowform.

Professions Relative to the Priest Class

Alchemy

  • Minor Arcane Elixir sell value reduced to 5 copper (was 25 copper).
  • Corrected the name of “Recipe: Elixir of Greater Firepower” to “Recipe: Elixir of Holy Power”, and the elixir’s aura is now called “Holy Power”.

Cooking

  • Journeyman Campfire Kit now requires Cooking 90 to place, matching its recipe skill requirement (was Cooking 140).

Enchanting

  • Arcane Salvager now requires the Runed Golden Rod tool to craft (was Runed Truesilver Rod).
  • Arcane Salvager now correctly applies its disenchanting bonus to lower-level enchanters.
  • Enchant Boots: Lesser Spirit and Enchant Bracer: Lesser Spirit now correctly give their stated bonus to Spirit (was Resist All).

Tailoring

Adjusted the required materials and slot size of several bags that were unintentionally smaller than intended:

  • Red Mageweave Bag: Now requires 5 bolts of mageweave (was 4 bolts) and is now 14 slots.
  • Green Silk Pack: Now requires 5 bolts of silk (was 4 bolts) and is now 12 slots.
  • Black Silk Pack: Now requires 6 bolts of silk (was 5 bolts) and is now 12 slots.
  • Green Woolen Bag: Now requires 5 bolts of wool (was 4 bolts) and is now 10 slots.
  • Red Woolen Bag: Now requires 5 bolts of wool (was 4 bolts) and is now 10 slots.

Engineering

  • Iron Grenades vendor price reduced to 1 silver 25 copper (was 5 silver).
  • Swiftstrike Shot and Swiftfeather Arrow are no longer Bind-on-Pickup.
    Developers' notes: These are not available until raids unlock, but we want to make sure this change is known, because it may influence profession choice. These were not intended to be Bind-on-Pickup.

Fishing

  • Fixed a condition mismatch that sometimes caused Fishing Racks to fail to provide lures to eligible players.
    Developers' notes: We are aware there are other ongoing issues with the Fishing Rack, including other situations that result in "There is no loot" errors.

title: The Priest Rollercoaster in World of Warcraft Forever and why Blizzard Needs to Separate PvE and PvP Balance
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Examining the volatile history of Priest balance in WoW Forever, the impact of knee-jerk PvP adjustments on PvE leveling, and why Blizzard must separate the two design ecosystems.
content:
If you play a Priest in World of Warcraft: Forever, the last few weeks have felt like a dizzying ride on a pendulum. We are caught in the crossfire of knee-jerk balance adjustments driven entirely by panic, shifting wildly between dominance and complete obscurity based on how classes perform in duels or low-level brackets.

The core issue is painfully clear: Blizzard needs to split PvE and PvP balancing. When developers try to use a single tuning knob for both environments, everyone suffers. PvE should have its own designated ecosystem, and PvP should be balanced separately, keeping classes on a level playing field without one aspect of the game entirely gutting another. Instead, we are left constantly dealing with overcorrections just to appease the vocal minority and the 1% of the audience, primarily streamers, while everyday players are forced to cope with the fallout.

The October 9th "D-Day" and Community Outcry

The turbulence reached a boiling point on October 9th, when Blizzard dropped a massive set of nerfs that sent the Priest community into a tailspin. Players took to the official forums to voice their utter disbelief at how hard the class was hit.

One angry forum user vented on October 9th:

"Blizzard keeps nerfing Priests into the ground. Over the past few weeks in beta, the boat has been rocking back and forward for everyone. But watching the duels in Durotar, and in one day's difference from the new nerf, the Priests are consistently losing in duels now unless it is Priest vs Priest, ret Pally, Warriors. That patch has been insane for Priests."

Another player highlighted the stark contrast between classes:

"Yeah, I am very confused by these nerfs. Priest may have been overperforming at level 30 PvP, but the PvE grind is a SLOG compared to classes like Hunters which go completely untouched."

While some acknowledged that Discipline priests at level 30 were exceptional healers, the counter-argument pointed out the catastrophic collateral damage done to their damage output:

"They were not tuned down a bit. They were gutted. If they had been tuned down a bit we would not be having this discussion. And the most concerning thing right now is the damage... right now we keep having to wand plus dot tab as the main thing to level. Penance damage was good before the nerf to the point that it was finally something new to cast while leveling, but in the nerf they gutted it too... Right now you can do more damage with your wand than a tick of penance. The only one functional thing they added to make priest leveling better got gutted. Back to wanding plus dot tabbing until 60."

The community was furious that sweeping adjustments were being made based on level 30 performance caps, forcing players back into the most monotonous leveling style imaginable just to satisfy purists who do not understand modern class tuning.

The October 15th Pivot: Walking It Back

The immense backlash forced Blizzard's hand, leading to a massive pivot in the October 15, 2026 patch notes to address the damage control:

  • Baseline Additions: Fear Ward and Devouring Plague became baseline for every Priest at level 20, with Divine Spirit moving to level 30 and Shadow Word: Death baseline at level 32.
  • Cooldown Reductions: Devouring Plague's cooldown dropped from 1 minute to 24 seconds, and Vampiric Embrace's cooldown dropped from 1 minute to 30 seconds while also becoming unresistable.
  • Quality of Life: Multiple Priests could finally keep Renew on the same target without higher ranks blocking it, and Prayer of Healing was updated to cover target party members and their pets.
  • Shadow Word: Death Adjustments: Set to deal instant Shadow damage while costing the Priest 30% of their maximum health if the target survived, removing the health penalty on a miss.

Blizzard even praised the class as the ultimate versatile healer, featuring direct heals, shields, and hots, yet noted that their low escape tools in cloth armor meant they heavily relied on friends for tanking and control.

Moving Into November: The November 3rd Tweaks

The saga continued into November, bringing further fine-tuning on November 3rd. Power Word: Shield mechanics were cleaned up, Undead Priest’s Dark Sacrifice had its crowd-break bug fixed, and Shadow Word: Death's self-damage penalty if failing to kill a target was bumped up to 30%.

On the talent front, Binding Heal was removed and replaced with Holy Binding, allowing 50% of the healing done by Flash Heal to also heal the Priest threat-free when targeting allies. Meanwhile, Shadow received fixes to prevent Devouring Contagion from spreading plague from critters, removed critical rolls on Vampiric Embrace healing, and fixed Cure and Abolish Disease from awkwardly knocking the Priest out of Shadowform.

Stop Catering to the 1%

The underlying frustration across all of this is that the development cycle is constantly hijacked by hyper-focused spotlight balancing. When balance teams react instantly to high-profile duels or streamer complaints, it destabilizes the core experience for everyone else.

It is time to separate PvE and PvP tuning permanently, stop the knee-jerk panic nerfs, and let us play our classes without living in fear of the next arbitrary patch notes. In a future article I will discuss how developers need to stop catering exclusively to the 1% streamer crowd.

title: The Darkmoon Faire Sets Up Shop in Elwynn Forest for WoW: Forever's Debut
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: The Darkmoon Faire is officially opening in Elwynn Forest for its debut in WoW Forever, bringing familiar attractions, Sayge's damage buff, and custom adjustments for raid settings.
content:
The iconic Darkmoon Faire is officially making its first-ever appearance in World of Warcraft: Forever, and the Alliance is starting things off with a major home-field advantage. The grounds are currently being assembled in Elwynn Forest, and according to the in-game calendar, the event goes live on Monday and will run for a full week.

For veterans of classic-era servers, the arrival of the Faire brings back all the familiar attractions: fun mini-games, reputation gains, and hard-to-find rewards. However, the biggest draw has always been Sayge's Dark Fortune of Damage, the famous fortune-telling buff that grants a 10% damage increase for two hours.

Things operate a bit differently in Forever, though. While world buffs are still fully functional out in the open world, developers have confirmed they will be barred from raids, altering how guilds approach endgame preparation.

Because this is the very first iteration of the Faire in Forever, the community is waiting to see if any new surprises or custom twists have been added to the grounds. We will find out just what kind of unique flair the development team has cooked up once the tents officially open their doors.

title: Blizzard Caves: WoW: Forever Hotfix Boosts Dungeon Mob XP by 50% After Massive Backlash
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Following intense community backlash over the one-and-done leveling meta, Blizzard deployed a live hotfix increasing WoW Forever dungeon mob experience gains by 50%.
content:
After a week of intense community uproar, heated forum debates, and widespread player frustration, Blizzard has officially blinked. A live hotfix deployed for World of Warcraft: Forever has boosted experience gains from dungeon creatures by a massive 50%.

The change marks a notable pivot for the development team, which had previously stood by a controversial philosophy: heavily nerfing mob experience inside dungeons while shifting the bulk of the leveling rewards into one-time dungeon quests.

The Rise of the "One-and-Done" Meta

When WoW: Forever launched its leveling ecosystem, players quickly realized that repeating dungeons was yielding remarkably low returns. Because mob experience had been drastically scaled down, the mathematical reality of dungeon crawling changed overnight.

The optimal playstyle quickly devolved into a rigid "one-and-done" strategy:

  • Players would form a group once to knock out all available dungeon quests.
  • Once the quests were handed in for a massive chunk of experience, the dungeon instantly lost its value.
  • Running the same instance a second or third time for loot, practice, or to help guildmates and friends felt fundamentally unrewarding.

This design choice fractured the community. Healers, tanks, and social players who preferred grouping up felt heavily penalized. Meanwhile, open-world questing zones became hyper-congested, leading to fierce tag-stealing and a general sentiment that a pillar of the classic experience: dungeon socialization: was being artificially choked out.

Community Reaction: Relief Mixed with Skepticism

While the official announcement was met with plenty of celebration from players eager to return to instance crawling, it also sparked a broader debate about balancing methodology.

Many veterans pointed out the sheer scale of the original reduction. Because the initial nerf slashed dungeon mob experience so deeply, a 50% buff still leaves overall mob values noticeably lower than historical baseline standards. Some community members voiced frustration that developers tend to use extreme adjustments: gutting values initially only to walk them back incrementally: rather than making measured modifications from the start.

Still, the overarching sentiment among players is one of immense relief. When a design choice actively discourages grouping up or helping guildmates through repetitive content, it misses the entire point of an MMORPG. Forcing a meta where people treat a dungeon like a single-player chore checklist completely strips away the social glue that keeps these worlds alive. Going back in for multiple runs won't feel nearly as punishing with this adjustment in place.

Looking Forward

The hotfix is already live, requiring no additional client downloads, and it arrives just ahead of further class tuning updates scheduled.

Whether this 50% increase is enough to satisfy die-hard dungeon spammers or if further adjustments will be required remains to be seen. For now, adventurers can queue up with friends, clear out trash packs, and hunt for those elusive low-level set pieces without feeling like they are actively wasting their leveling time.

title: Mastering the 25% Wand Rule & Why Every Caster Needs a Wand ASAP in WoW Forever
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Master the 25% wand rule, the 5-Second Rule, and Spirit Tap mechanics. Learn how to craft or buy your first wand early to eliminate drinking downtime in WoW Forever.
content:
If you are playing a Priest, Mage, or Warlock in World of Warcraft: Forever, let me give you the single biggest piece of leveling advice that transformed my entire experience: get a wand the absolute second you hit 3 to 5 silver.

I'll admit it: I'm in love with this playstyle. On my Priest leveling journey, picking up an early wand completely flipped a switch. No mana used, no casting delays, no fuss, and no muss. You can step into the open world, target non-elite mobs and non-players, and take them down remarkably fast with just your wand. Early on, wanding isn't just a mana-saver: it is literally faster than casting regular spells over and over.

Here is the exact strategy for using your wand to abuse the 5-Second Rule and Spirit Tap, plus where to get your first wand on a fresh server budget.

Understanding the 25% Rule, the 5-Second Rule, and Spirit Tap

For Priests and other casters in classic-style client mechanics, mana efficiency revolves around one core mechanic: The 5-Second Rule (5SR). Natural mana regeneration completely pauses while casting and for 5 seconds after spending any mana.

This is where the 25% Rule comes into play:

  • The Opener: Open a fight by spending your mana upfront: apply your Damage-Over-Time spells (like Shadow Word: Pain) or 1–2 heavy offensive casts.
  • The Wand Finish: Once the mob reaches roughly the last 25% to 30% of its health, stop casting entirely and switch strictly to your wand.
  • Triggering 5SR & Spirit Tap: Because using a wand costs zero mana, your 5-second timer expires while you are finishing off the mob. The exact moment the mob dies, two huge things happen simultaneously: your natural mana regeneration is already fully active because 5 seconds have passed since your last spell, and Spirit Tap triggers on the kill shot, doubling your Spirit and massively boosting your mana regen rate.

By doing this, you enter the next pull at 100% mana without ever having to stop and drink. It creates a seamless, zero-downtime leveling engine.

What does "Required Level" mean? The level listed on a wand (e.g., Level 5) is the minimum Character Level required to equip it. It has nothing to do with your profession level.

Method 1: The Crafting Shortcut (~2 Silver, 50 Copper)

If you don't want to rely on the Auction House economy on launch night, you can craft a starter wand yourself by making a quick trip to your faction's main city or nearest Enchanting trainer.

In WoW Forever, Blizzard introduced the Novice's Practice Wand, which allows fresh casters to bypass early RNG and craft a usable weapon entirely from vendor-bought materials.

Shopping List & Materials

To craft your first wand at Enchanting Skill Level 1, you will need approximately 2s 50c total to cover training fees and vendor items:

  • Copper Rod (Purchased from Enchanting Supplies vendor)
  • 2x Mote of Magic (Purchased from Enchanting Supplies vendor: 1 for your rod, 1 for the wand)
  • 1x Simple Wood (Purchased from Trade or Enchanting Supplies vendor)

The Crafting Steps

  1. Learn Enchanting (Skill 1).
  2. Craft the Runed Copper Rod using 1x Copper Rod + 1x Mote of Magic.
  3. Craft the Novice's Practice Wand using 1x Simple Wood + 1x Mote of Magic.

Once you hit Enchanting level 10, you can upgrade to the Lesser Magic Wand (requires 1x Simple Wood + 1x Lesser Magic Essence).

Method 2: The Auction House Route

If you prefer to skip profession training entirely, save up your silver and head straight to the Auction House in the nearest main city. On fresh server economies, early crafted wands are heavily traded and usually priced very fairly.

Here is what early wand pricing looks like across character level brackets:

  • Novice's Practice Wand (Level 1): ~1s – 2s (Great starting baseline)
  • Lesser Magic Wand (Level 5): ~2s (Must-Buy Target: Huge DPS spike early)
  • Fire Wand (Level 7): ~3s (Solid mid-tier upgrade)
  • Shadow Wand (Level 9): ~5s (Strong option for Priests/Warlocks)
  • Blazing Wand (Level 12): ~7s (Good DPS, but pricier)
  • Greater Magic Wand (Level 13): ~3s – 5s (Fantastic power bump once hit)

My Personal Setup: I purchased a Lesser Magic Wand at Level 9 for just 2 silver, and it was an immediate game-changer for my Priest. While higher-level options like the Blazing Wand (Level 12) or Greater Magic Wand (Level 13) hit harder, I strongly recommend securing a wand at the earliest level possible (Level 5–7) rather than waiting. The momentum you gain in kill speed and saved drinking time far outweighs waiting for a slightly higher stat bar later.

My Advice

Don't sit around waiting for a lucky drop in a starting zone. The moment your pouch holds 3 to 5 silver, either make the run to the Enchanting trainer or check the Auction House. Grab your wand, hit auto-attack on those open-world mobs to finish them off, and let your Spirit Tap engine do the rest.

title: Technical Chaos, Blizzard Weather, and Launch Night Magic: My First 48 Hours in WoW Forever
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: From a launch night client freeze and fixing the Spirit Tap Engine under fire to experiencing dynamic blizzard weather in Dun Morogh, here is the recap of the first 48 hours in WoW Forever.
content:
When the servers for World of Warcraft: Forever finally opened, I did what any self-respecting Priest main would do: I tried to log in instantly.

My initial play was an Undead Priest on the PvE server. I hit create, got the confirmation screen, and then... complete freeze. Client locked up, forcing a hard task-kill. Classic launch night energy.

Three hours in the queue later, I finally crossed the threshold into Azeroth: only to immediately run into an addon engineer's worst nightmare.

Fixing the Engine Under Fire

The moment I loaded in, my Spirit Tap Engine was completely broken.

Now, this isn't some unvalidated side project: this engine worked seamlessly across WoW Classic, Season of Discovery, and multiple other iterations of the client. But Forever brought its own subtle API shifts under the hood, and launch night didn't care about backward compatibility.

I spent the next two hours completely stripping down the codebase line by line, re-architecting the broken components, and rebuilding it from the ground up. Two hours of high-stakes debugging while the rest of the world was out tagging mobs. By the time I pushed the fix, it was rock-solid, workable, and ready for the public to run.

Double-Dipping Azeroth

With the engine back online, the real journey began. I immediately switched gears to set up my long-term roster:

  • Dwarf Priest (PvP Server): Built for the high-stakes open-world grind.
  • Dwarf Priest (PvE Server): Created specifically for launch night to duo-level alongside my brother, who is maining a Dwarf Hunter.

Stepping into Dun Morogh on launch night hit differently this time around. Blizzard’s upgraded weather effects in WoW Forever are genuinely breathtaking. Running through a dynamic, complete white-out blizzard with visibility cut down and snow swirling across the terrain made the starting zone feel wildly immersive: a proper reminder of why we fell in love with world-driven gaming in the first place.

The 48-Hour Grind

Over the past two days, it’s been total head-down focus. Balancing two separate Priest characters requires real discipline, but the rhythm has been unreal:

  • Leveling Efficiency: Pushing levels across both characters through coordinated duo-grinding and strategic solo routes.
  • Profession Foundation: Getting tradeskills locked in early to feed gear and consumable loops down the road.
  • Financial Management: Playing smart with every silver piece on fresh-server economies where early capital dictates mid-game control.
  • Streaming the Journey: Broadcasting the entire ride live, sharing the wins, the technical hotfixes, and the raw launch energy with the community.

What's Next on the Workbench?

Launch night threw a frozen client and a broken codebase at the door, but working through the chaos and stepping into a blizzard-laden Dun Morogh made night one unforgettable.

And for everyone following along: consider this a spoiler alert. Fixing Spirit Tap Engine under fire was just phase one: I already have another Priest-focused addon in active development coming very soon. Stay tuned to the stream and site as the code comes together.

WoW Forever is officially here, and we're set to go.

title: Spell Power, Hit & Crit: Maximizing Priest Damage and Shield Scaling
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Dive into coefficient mechanics, hit caps, and crit interactions for Priests. Learn how Spell Power scales your damage and shields, and how Divine Aegis turns critical heals into massive protective buffers.
content:
Spell Power, Hit & Crit: Maximizing Priest Scaling

Once you transition past basic leveling stats and step into high-level dungeons and raids, raw throughput depends entirely on understanding secondary scaling. For Priests, managing Spell Power coefficients, hit caps, and critical strike interactions is what separates average healers and casters from elite performers.

Spell Power & Coefficient Mechanics

Spell Power does not always translate to a 1:1 damage or healing increase. Every spell in the game utilizes a specific coefficient based on its cast time, balancing instant-cast utility against long cast-time power.

  • Direct Cast Spells: Spells with standard 3.0-second cast times, such as Greater Heal or Mind Blast, receive 100% of your total Spell Power bonus.
  • Channeled & Periodic Spells: Spells like Mind Flay or Shadow Word: Pain distribute their Spell Power scaling across their total duration, making haste and duration modifiers critical for DPS output.
  • Power Word: Shield Scaling: Shield absorption scales directly with your healing/spell power, meaning stacking high Spell Power gear turns your shields into formidable mitigation walls that absorb massive boss damage before it reaches your target's health bar.
Verdict: Prioritize raw Spell Power once your baseline mana sustain and Spirit thresholds are met to maximize your output per cast.

Hit Chance: Eliminating Resistances

In raid encounters against boss targets (Level 63), spell resistance can drastically lower your overall damage and threat generation.

  • The Base Cap: Casters require a baseline 16% spell hit chance against raid bosses to completely eliminate spell misses.
  • Shadow Focus Synergy: Investing points into the Shadow Focus talent reduces your spell hit requirement significantly for shadow spells, easing your gear budgeting.
  • The Cost of Misses: A resisted Shadow Word: Pain or Mind Blast not only wastes valuable mana but also breaks your damage rotation and Shadow Weaving uptime.

Critical Strike & Divine Aegis Synergy

Critical strikes do more than just deal extra damage; they unlock powerful defensive and offensive mechanics across your talent tree.

  • Divine Aegis Interaction: For Discipline Priests, Divine Aegis converts non-periodic critical heals into a protective shield on the target equal to a percentage of the healing done. Stacking critical strike chance directly multiplies your active mitigation.
  • Shadowform Crits: Staying in Shadowform boosts your shadow critical strike chance, feeding into mana-regeneration procs and high burst windows.

title: Spirit vs. Intellect: The Priest Leveling & Mana Regeneration War
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: Mastering early Priest mana sustain comes down to Spirit versus Intellect. Learn how the 5-Second Rule and Spirit Tap dictate your uptime, along with key stat priorities by level bracket.
content:
The Priest Leveling & Mana Regeneration War

When leveling a Priest in World of Warcraft, two primary stats dictate your speed and uptime: Intellect and Spirit. While both build out your mana pool and sustain, stacking them incorrectly will force you to sit down and drink after every single mob pull. Understanding how these two stats interact, and when to prioritize one over the other, is the key to continuous, zero-downtime pulling.

Intellect: Max Mana & Early Critical Strike

Intellect is your raw engine capacity. It directly increases your maximum mana pool and provides a minor boost to your spell critical strike chance.

  • Mana Pool Sizing: Each point of Intellect grants 15 maximum mana.
  • Critical Strike Scaling: It takes roughly 59.5 points of Intellect to gain 1% Spell Critical Strike chance.
  • The Leveling Reality: A larger mana pool is great for bursting down single targets or panic-healing in dungeons, but it does not make you regenerate mana any faster during combat.
Verdict: Intellect gives you a larger gas tank, but it doesn't improve your fuel efficiency.

Spirit: The Uptime & Regeneration Engine

Spirit is the ultimate leveling stat for Priests. It drives your health and mana recovery rate, scaling directly with core Priest talent mechanics.

  • Out-of-Combat Regeneration: Spirit dictates how fast your health and mana bounce back between pulls.
  • The 5-Second Rule (5SR): Mana regen pauses for 5 seconds after spending mana on a spell cast. Spirit dictates how rapidly your mana ticks back up the second that 5-second window closes.
  • Spirit Tap Synergy: Scoring a killing blow triggers Spirit Tap, doubling your Spirit and granting 100% mana regeneration while casting for 15 seconds. High Spirit during a Spirit Tap window completely refills your pool while you wand down the next mob.
Verdict: Spirit is your fuel efficiency. Stacking Spirit keeps your wand swinging and eliminates drinking breaks entirely.

Stat Priority by Level Bracket

  • Levels 1–20 (Spirit > Intellect): Rush 5/5 Wand Specialization and 5/5 Spirit Tap. Cast 1–2 spells early, then wand to let Spirit regen your pool during the 5-Second Rule.
  • Levels 21–40 (Spirit >= Intellect): Balance Spirit with enough Intellect to sustain multi-dotting or early dungeon healing runs.
  • Levels 41–60 (Intellect / Spell Power > Spirit): As your spell coefficients scale and you pick up Meditation (or go heavy Shadow), raw Spell Power and Intellect take over for faster kill times.

title: Latest WoW Forever Beta Priest Class Changes 10/15
author: Lawrentiueus
summary: The latest WoW Forever Beta patch brings significant class updates for Priests. Highlights include major cooldown changes for Devouring Plague and Vampiric Embrace, talent tree reshuffling across Discipline and Shadow, key bug fixes, and the brand-new party Spirit buffing talent: Dark Inspiration.
content:
General Priest Changes

Spell Adjustments & Quality of Life

  • Renew: Fixed an issue where high ranks of Renew were preventing other Priests from applying Renew to the target.
  • Holy Fire: Fixed an issue causing Rank 5 periodic damage to be higher than Rank 6.
  • Power Word: Shield: Will now correctly tell the player they can’t replace a Power Word: Shield on a target if the active shield is stronger.
  • Power Word: Shield: Fixed an issue where casting Power Word: Shield would say SHIELDED twice in scrolling combat text.
  • Mind Vision: Fixed an issue where casting Mind Vision would cause the target to stand up and interrupt drinks.

Cooldown Updates

  • Devouring Plague: Cooldown reduced to 24 seconds (was 1 minute).
  • Shadow Word: Death: Cooldown increased to 18 seconds (was 12 seconds).

Discipline Tree Changes

Ability Mechanics & Tooltips

  • Inner Focus: Will now correctly only be used on a single spell, even if you spell queue another spell into Penance’s channel.
  • Divine Aegis: Tooltip explicitly updated to state that it is activated by Non-Periodic critical heals.
  • Divine Aegis: Tooltip now explicitly lists the maximum value for the shield.
  • Power in Light: Now increases Smite and Penance if the target is afflicted by Holy Fire or Shadow Word: Pain.
  • Silent Resolve: Threat reduction now applies to all spells.

Talent Tree Reshuffling

  • Mental Strength: Moved to Row 2 from Row 4. Changed to increase your Intellect by 2/4/6/8/10%.
  • Improved Power Word: Shield: Moved to Row 3 from Row 2.
  • Twin Disciplines: Now correctly benefits Shadow Word: Death, Mind Flay, Starshards, and Penance.

Shadow Tree Changes

Bug Fixes & Core Adjustments

  • Shadow Word: Death: Fixed an issue where it was not benefitting from Shadowform’s increase to critical strike damage.
  • Devouring Contagion: Fixed an issue where the bounced Devouring Plague was costing Mana, performing a cast animation, and putting the caster’s Devouring Plague back on full cooldown.
  • Vampiric Embrace: Changed so that it can’t be resisted. Cooldown reduced to 30 seconds (was 1 minute).
  • Shadow Weaving: Tooltip fixed to correctly state that it causes the target to take increased damage from you.

Talent Reworks & New Additions

  • NEW TALENT Dark Inspiration (Row 4): Your Mind Blast and fully channeled Mind Flay cause Dark Inspiration, increasing yours and your party’s Spirit by 3/6/9/12/15% for 10 seconds.
  • Improved Mind Flay: Changed to, each instance of damage of Mind Flay deals 10/20% more damage than its previous instance of damage.
  • Devouring Contagion: Now spreads to 2 targets.
  • Improved Mind Blast: Moved from Row 3 to Row 2.
  • REMOVED Improved Fade: Removed from the talent tree.
  • REMOVED Shadow Infinity: Removed from the talent tree.
